title: Dry, grade, pack and prove it: adding value after harvest
course_title: Agribusiness and Market Access: Grade, Store and Sell Your Produce for a Better Price

say: Dry, grade, pack and prove it. Adding value after harvest.
This is the video for module two of Agribusiness and Market Access.
Most of the extra money a farmer can earn is won or lost in the days after harvest. Done carelessly, handling causes mould, insects, bruising and weight loss.

say: Done well, it gives you produce buyers trust and pay more for. And simple records prove whether your changes really raised your income.

say: Wet grain is the root of most storage problems. For maize, about 13% moisture or lower is usually recommended for safe storage. Dry on a clean tarpaulin, never on bare earth or the roadside, and turn it several times a day.
To test, fill a clean, dry jar about one third with grain from several places in the heap.

say: If salt sticks to the inside, the grain is still too wet. Keep drying and test again. If the salt falls freely, it is dry enough in most cases.

say: Grading means sorting produce into groups of similar quality, so a buyer knows exactly what she is getting. Here is Grace. These prices are illustrative.
Sold mixed, her 30 crates bring 420,000 naira.
She sorts them: 18 crates of firm Grade A, 9 of Grade B, and 3 soft crates for soup sellers. Together they bring 459,000 naira.

say: Now safety. Aflatoxins are poisons from moulds on maize, groundnuts and other grains and nuts. Long-term exposure is linked to liver cancer, and normal cooking does not reliably destroy them.
Harvest on time, dry fast, remove mouldy grain, and never sell it, eat it or feed it to animals.

cards.d: Poison from mould on badly dried grain and nuts. Cooking does not remove it. Never sell or eat mouldy grain.
Follow the label. Wait the pre-harvest interval. Gloves, mask, long sleeves. Never spray into the wind.
Aluminium phosphide gas has killed households. Never keep or use it. Licensed operators only.

say: Every pesticide label states the pre-harvest interval, the days you must wait between the last spray and harvest. Wear protection, never spray into the wind, and never store chemicals in food or drink containers.

say: Never keep grain storage tablets such as aluminium phosphide in or near your home, and never use them yourself. Use hermetic bags or methods your extension officer advises.

say: Overfilled raffia baskets crush the fruit at the bottom. Halima lost about 20% of her loads that way. A group member using crates loses about 5%.
That saves 6 loads a season. At about 15,000 naira a load, that is 90,000 naira.
Twenty crates cost about 100,000 naira, so they pay for themselves in just over one season, and she reuses them for several more.

Buyers quote in bags, baskets and mudu, so divide every price by the weight in kilograms. Ngozi's offer of 62,000 naira for a 100 kg bag is 620 naira a kilo. 32,500 naira for a 50 kg bag sounds smaller, but it is 650 naira a kilo, the better deal.

say: To remember. Dry grain on a tarpaulin and test it before storing. Grade so your best produce earns more. Never sell or eat mouldy grain. Respect the pre-harvest interval on every label. And compare net naira per kilogram.
